nameStory: The bloody-heart lichen gets its dramatic name from a hidden surprise — when the gray surface is scratched or damaged, it reveals a bright carmine-red cushion underneath, like discovering a beating heart beneath pale skin. This crimson 'bleeding' effect makes it unmistakable once you know what to look for.
description: Bloody-heart lichen is a crusty, gray lichen that forms irregular patches on tree bark, looking somewhat like dried oatmeal or rough concrete. The surface appears bumpy and warty, often cracking as it ages, and can range from pale gray to darker charcoal tones. It's distinguished by black, dome-shaped fruiting bodies that dot the surface, and most remarkably, the bright red tissue that shows when the lichen is damaged. These patches can grow quite large over many years, sometimes covering significant portions of a tree trunk.

idTips.label: Hidden Red Heart
idTips.description: Gently scratch or scrape the gray surface with a fingernail — bright carmine-red tissue will be revealed underneath, like discovering hidden blood beneath gray skin

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms thick, crusty patches that feel rough and bumpy to the touch, like coarse sandpaper or dried oatmeal stuck to bark

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Surface is distinctly warty and uneven, often cracked into irregular sections, with a thick, substantial feel when pressed

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale to dark gray overall, sometimes with a slightly bluish tint, remaining fairly consistent whether wet or dry

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Black, shiny fruiting bodies (apothecia) become dome-shaped or hemispherical as they mature, sitting prominently on the red cushions

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost always found growing directly on tree bark, particularly favoring the trunks and larger branches of forest trees

habitat: Look for bloody-heart lichen on the bark of trees in temperate and mountain forests throughout New England, from lowland woods to higher elevations. It seems to prefer the trunks and main branches of mature trees, where it can establish the thick, substantial colonies it's known for. Occasionally it may be found on old, weathered wood or moss-covered rocks, but tree bark is definitely its favorite home.

seasonality.spring: The gray patches remain visible and identifiable year-round. Spring moisture may make the colors slightly more vibrant, and the red heart tissue shows just as dramatically when scratched.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer weather, the lichen may appear more muted in color, but the diagnostic red tissue underneath remains bright and easy to reveal with gentle scraping.
seasonality.fall: Fall rains can intensify the gray coloration slightly, and the contrast with the hidden red tissue becomes particularly striking against autumn's colorful backdrop.
seasonality.winter: Completely visible and identifiable in winter, when the lack of leaves makes it easier to spot on tree trunks. Snow and ice don't hide the telltale red bleeding when the surface is disturbed.

funFact: This lichen is essentially carrying around its own first aid kit — the bright red tissue that bleeds when damaged contains special compounds that help protect and heal the wound, just like how our blood clots and scabs form when we're injured!
confusionNotes: Many gray crusty lichens look similar on first glance, but the scratch test with a fingernail is foolproof — only bloody-heart lichen will bleed that distinctive bright red. Remember: "Gray and crusty? Give it a scratch-y!"
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "bloody-heart," this lichen is completely harmless and the red substance won't stain your fingers permanently. The scientific name "sanguinarius" literally means "bloody," reinforcing that this red-bleeding characteristic has been its defining feature for centuries.
compareHints: The closely related Mycoblastus sanguinarioides is extremely similar and also bleeds red when scratched, making them very difficult to tell apart in the field. Both have the same gray, warty appearance and red interior tissue, so definitive identification between these two species typically requires microscopic examination or chemical testing by experts.
